modules.name: BigNat
modules.header:
An arbitrary-size natural number, for the two conversions that have to be exact.
Turning a float into its shortest decimal, or a decimal into the nearest float, is a question about where the
exact value sits between two neighbours, and answering it with floating-point arithmetic loses the very bits the
answer depends on. The classic way out is integer arithmetic on the exact value: a float is an integer times a
power of two, a decimal is an integer times a power of ten, and comparing the two needs nothing more than big
integers that can be multiplied, shifted and compared. That is everything this type does, and nothing more.
The sizes involved are why this cannot be a fixed width. A float512 reaches 2^4194303, and the exact decimal
conversion of a value near that limit works on numbers of that many bits. They come from an allocator because
nothing else can hold them; the narrow widths never get near that, and a float80 never needs more than a few
hundred words.

modules.name: Bool128
modules.header:
A `bool128` is the word `true` or the word `false`.
The fifth boolean width renders exactly as the other four do. A boolean's text has nothing to do with how many
bytes it is stored in, and a width that rendered differently would be a width a caller had to remember.

modules.header:

modules.name: Char128
modules.header:
A `char128` holds one Unicode scalar value in sixteen bytes, which is one to four bytes of UTF-8.
It is a `char64` with more room for numbers no character has. A scalar value stops at U+10FFFF, so every bit
above the twenty-first is zero in a real character, and a cast that sets one makes a value that is no character
at all. The check runs at the full 128 bits, before anything is narrowed: dropping the high word first would
turn a value whose low bits spell `A` into that `A`.

modules.name: Char16
modules.header:
A `char16` holds one UTF-16 code unit, which is one to three bytes of UTF-8.
A code unit that is half of a surrogate pair says nothing on its own: the character it belongs to is spread across
two of them, and one of them is all this sees. So it is written as the replacement character rather than as an
ill-formed sequence.

modules.name: Char256
modules.header:
A `char256` holds one Unicode scalar value in thirty-two bytes, which is one to four bytes of UTF-8.
It is a `char64` with more room for numbers no character has. A scalar value stops at U+10FFFF, so every bit
above the twenty-first is zero in a real character, and a cast that sets one makes a value that is no character
at all. The check runs at the full 256 bits, before anything is narrowed: dropping the high words first would
turn a value whose low bits spell `A` into that `A`.

modules.name: Char32
modules.header:
A `char32` holds one Unicode scalar value, which is one to four bytes of UTF-8.
A `char32` is checked when it is made, so a value that is not a scalar value cannot ordinarily be in one. It is
still checked here, because a cast can produce one and the writer's promise is worth more than the check costs.

modules.name: Char512
modules.header:
A `char512` holds one Unicode scalar value in sixty-four bytes, which is one to four bytes of UTF-8.
It is a `char64` with more room for numbers no character has. A scalar value stops at U+10FFFF, so every bit
above the twenty-first is zero in a real character, and a cast that sets one makes a value that is no character
at all. The check runs at the full 512 bits, before anything is narrowed: dropping the high words first would
turn a value whose low bits spell `A` into that `A`.

modules.name: Char64
modules.header:
A `char64` holds one Unicode scalar value in eight bytes, which is one to four bytes of UTF-8.
The width is the whole difficulty. A scalar value stops at U+10FFFF and a `char64` has room for four billion
times that, so a cast can put a number in one that no character has. Checking after narrowing to `uint32` would
be worse than not checking: `0x100000041` narrows to `0x41`, which is a perfectly good `A`, and the wrong
character is harder to notice than a refused one. So validity is decided at the full sixty-four bits, before
anything is narrowed.

modules.name: Char8
modules.header:
A `char8` is one byte of UTF-8, which is not the same thing as one character.
A byte below 0x80 is a whole character and is written as it stands. A byte above that is one piece of a character
spread over several, and a writer takes whole characters — so what is written for one is the replacement
character, U+FFFD, which is what "there was something here and it could not be represented" looks like in text.
Writing the byte on its own would produce something that is not UTF-8, and the promise that it is holds every
reader of the result together.

modules.name: CharacterSlice
modules.header:
Character slices render their bytes directly, without conversion or copying. The caller supplies valid UTF-8
when the result is intended as text; an arbitrary character slice carries no validity guarantee.
`Debug` is where the two partings show. Text shown to a reader is its characters; text shown to somebody looking
at a program is quoted, so that where it starts and stops is visible and an empty string is not invisible.
This file is the `char8[..]` half, which renders by being copied: it is already the encoding the destination
wants. `char16[..]` and `char32[..]` each need a transcoding printer and have one in `WideCharacterSlice.rux`,
where the decisions about units that are not characters live.

modules.name: CharacterText
modules.header:
What the character widths and character slices share: the replacement rule, and the escape that undoes it.
Every character width has values that are not characters. A `char8` above 0x7F is one piece of a character
spread over several; a `char16` in the surrogate range is half of one; a `char32` or any wider width can be cast
from a number that is no scalar value at all. There is one rule for all of them and it has two halves.
`Display` replaces. A value that is not a whole character is written as U+FFFD, which is what "there was
something here and it could not be represented" looks like in text, and it keeps the promise every reader of the
output relies on: what comes out is well-formed UTF-8. That is lossy, and it is meant to be — two different
invalid values render alike, and neither can be read back.
`Debug` preserves. It is the rendering for somebody looking at a program rather than reading its output, and
telling them U+FFFD tells them nothing they did not already know. So an invalid value is written as an escape
carrying its own number — `'\x{80}'` for a stray byte, `'\u{d800}'` for a lone surrogate — and every value can
be told from every other. That is the same split, and the same escape spellings, that `Rux/Path` uses for a
native name, and for the same reason.
Neither half is a validation. `Text`'s strict conversions still refuse what is not text, and a value that
reaches a `Display` implementation has already passed whatever check its own type applies; the replacement here
is presentation, and never a substitute for the check.

modules.name: Cursor
modules.header:
A fixed run of bytes being filled from the front.
Every primitive has a longest possible rendering that is known in advance — twenty digits for a `uint64`, a
handful more for a float's sign, point and exponent — so the digits go into a buffer on the stack and reach the
writer in one call. Nothing here allocates, which is the point: printing a number should not need an allocator to
exist, let alone succeed.
A cursor that runs out stops writing rather than overrunning, and says so. Every caller in this package sizes its
buffer from the same bound the formatter is written against, so running out means the bound is wrong; refusing
silently would turn that into a truncated number, which is worse than an obvious one.

modules.name: Decimal
modules.header:
The float conversions all funnel through here. What separates a float32
from a float64 is only how many digits it can carry before the noise of
the binary representation shows through, so that count is a parameter and
the machinery below is shared.

modules.name: Digits
modules.header:
The digit loop, written once.
Every signed integer widens to `int64` on the way in and every unsigned one to `uint64`, neither of which loses
anything, so there is one loop rather than one per width.
The digits go into a cursor over a stack buffer rather than into anything that allocates: a `uint64` is at most
twenty digits, which is known before the loop starts, so there is nothing to grow and nothing that can fail.

modules.name: FixedNat
modules.header:
An unsigned integer of fixed capacity, for the float conversion that may not allocate.
`BigNat` next door grows and takes an allocator, which is right for the wide widths and wrong here: an ordinary
`Display` is reached from a placeholder in the middle of writing something else, and a rendering that can fail
for want of memory makes every `{}` fallible for a reason that has nothing to do with the value. So the narrow
widths convert in storage whose size is fixed when this file is compiled.
Sixty-four limbs of sixty-four bits is 4,096 bits, against a worst case of 3,681 — the denominator a decimal
with the full retained digit count and a tiny exponent is read over, `10^1108`. The derivation is in
Docs/NarrowFloat.md, with the five other quantities it was taken as the largest of. That leaves 415 bits of
headroom, over six limbs.
One size serves both directions. Rendering needs only 1,131 bits and would fit in twenty limbs, but a second
workspace would mean a second derivation and a second set of proofs to keep true, and the cost of the larger
one is stack rather than allocation.
Every operation that could pass the capacity answers whether it did, and a refused one leaves the value exactly
as it was. None of them truncates, wraps or saturates: a wrong answer from an exact algorithm is worse than no
answer, because the whole point of the method is that there is nothing to approximate and so nothing to be
slightly wrong about. A caller that sees `false` has hit a value the bound was proved not to reach, which is a
defect in the bound rather than an input to handle — and it can look at the value it still has to say so.
Leaving the value alone costs a copy only where it could matter. An operation whose result needs at most one
more limb cannot overflow a workspace that is not already full, so the common path writes in place; only a
workspace at its capacity does the work in a local copy and commits it on success. The copy happens on the path
that is about to report a defect anyway.

modules.name: Float16
modules.header:
The text of a `float16`.
The shortest decimal that reads back as the same `float16`, found at this width's own neighbours: 0.1 is stored
as 0.0999755859375, and the shortest decimal no other `float16` is closer to is "0.1", where measuring against
the `float32` the value widens to would ask for "0.099975586". A precision in the placeholder asks for fixed
notation instead, and the `e` and `E` styles for scientific notation, through the same writers as the wider
widths.
There is no hardware arithmetic for this width on the targets Rux supports, so the classification below reads
the bits rather than comparing values: it costs a mask instead of a call into the software comparison.

modules.name: Float32
modules.header:
The text of a `float32`.
The shortest decimal that reads back as the same value, which is what a reader almost always wants: 0.1 prints as
"0.1" rather than as the seventeen digits its binary value really is. A precision in the placeholder asks for
fixed notation instead, and is honoured exactly when the value has that many digits to give; the `e` and `E`
styles ask for scientific notation.

modules.name: Float64
modules.header:
The text of a `float64`.
The shortest decimal that reads back as the same value, so 0.1 prints as "0.1" rather than as the seventeen
digits its binary value really is — and it is the shortest one exactly, found by the digit generator in
ShortestDigits.rux rather than by rounding to a fixed count and hoping. A precision in the placeholder asks for
fixed notation instead, and the `e` and `E` styles for scientific notation, both written in Scientific.rux and
PrecisionDigits.rux.

modules.name: Float8
modules.header:
The text of a `float8`.
The shortest decimal that reads back as the same `float8`, found at this width's own neighbours: 0.1 is stored
as 0.1015625, and the shortest decimal no other `float8` is closer to is "0.1", where measuring against the
`float32` the value widens to would ask for all seven digits. The layout is E4M3 with IEEE-style specials: four
bits of significand, an exponent biased by seven, and the all-ones exponent kept for the infinities and NaNs.
A precision in the placeholder asks for fixed notation instead, and the `e` and `E` styles for scientific
notation, through the same writers as the wider widths.
There is no hardware arithmetic for this width on the targets Rux supports, so the classification below reads
the bits rather than comparing values: it costs a mask instead of a call into the software comparison.

modules.name: FloatDigits
modules.header:
Taking a narrow float apart, and putting its shortest digits back together as text.
The bits are read through a pointer rather than through a conversion, because there is no conversion that
preserves them: casting a `float64` to a `uint64` asks for the value's integer part, and what is wanted is its
representation. That is a documented unsafe boundary, the same one NarrowParse.rux crosses to turn bits back
into a float and WideFloatValue.rux crosses to bridge the wide primitives.
What comes out is the significand and the power of two it is scaled by, in the form the exact digit generator
takes. A subnormal has a zero exponent field and no implicit leading bit; a normal has the bit and an exponent
biased by the format. The third thing the generator needs is whether the value sits at the bottom of its
binade — where its lower neighbour is half as far away as its upper one, because the exponent steps down
underneath it. That is the stored mantissa being zero, with the exception of the smallest normal, whose lower
neighbour is the largest subnormal and is a full gap away like any other.

modules.name: Format
modules.header:
Filling placeholders in a run of text.
`{}` takes the next argument, in the order they are written; `{:spec}` carries a specification, parsed once by
Text and applied by the value; `{{` and `}}` are how a literal brace is spelled. That is the whole grammar, and
anything else containing a brace is a mistake in the pattern rather than text to copy through.
Strictness is the decision this file rests on, and it replaces two lenient behaviours that used to live here. A
placeholder with no argument left used to render as nothing, and a specification that did not parse used to be
copied through as literal text. Both reported the mistake by printing it, which is the worst of the options: the
program carries on, the output is wrong in a way that looks deliberate, and the caller finds out from a reader.
Both are now failures — `ArgumentCountMismatch` and `InvalidSpecification` — and both are found before anything
is written, so a pattern that is wrong produces no output at all rather than a prefix of one.
Finding them first is why the pattern is walked twice. The first pass validates: it counts the placeholders,
parses every specification, and rejects a brace that is not part of the grammar, without touching the
destination. The second pass writes. A pattern is small and the parse is a few comparisons per placeholder, so
the cost is the price of never emitting half a rendering of a pattern that was never going to work.
Arguments arrive as `Display`, so each one writes itself into the destination directly. Nothing is rendered into
a string on the way, which is what keeps the allocation count at what the result itself needs.

modules.name: Int
modules.header:
The decimal text of an `int`.
A negative value opens with a minus sign; a positive one carries no sign, since a sign that is always there is
noise and one that is there on request belongs to the placeholder rather than the value.

modules.name: IntegerText
modules.header:
Spelling an integer: sign, base prefix, zero padding and digits, in that order.
This is what is left in Format once the text-only half of padding moved into Text. Measuring a rendering and
writing fill around it is a text operation and lives there as `WriteAligned`; deciding that `-7` at width four is
`-007` rather than `00-7` is a fact about how a number is spelled, and lives here.
The two interlock through `PaddingAround`, which hands back the two fill counts without requiring the rendered
text to exist anywhere as one run. That matters: a number goes out as sign, then prefix, then zeros, then digits,
each straight to the writer, so the widest integer costs no more storage than its own digit buffer.

modules.name: NarrowParse
modules.header:
Reading a decimal into the nearest narrow float, exactly.
The other half of the same claim the renderer makes. The renderer writes the shortest decimal that reads back as
the same bits; this reads a decimal into the float nearest it, with ties to even, and between them the pair
closes. The old reader scaled in floating point and was wrong across a good part of the exponent range — it read
back the largest finite `float64` as a different value than it had been given — which is what made the round
trip a claim about the middle of the range rather than about the range.
The value is formed as an exact ratio, `digits / 10^-exponent` or `digits * 10^exponent`, scaled into [1, 2),
and the significand's bits are taken from it by long division. What the division leaves is the tail, held
exactly, so "is it more than half" is a comparison rather than an estimate and a tie is a tie rather than a
value that landed near one. A tie goes to the even significand.
Long input is where an exact reader has to decide something. Digits are retained up to a bound and anything
beyond sets a sticky flag, and the bound is chosen so that the flag is enough: an exact midpoint between two
floats is a dyadic rational, its decimal expansion terminates, and the longest one a `float64` has runs to 768
significant digits. So a nonzero digit past the 768th means the value is strictly above the retained one and
strictly between two midpoints, which rounds one way with no tie to resolve. Below that bound the retained
digits are the value exactly and a tie really is a tie.

modules.name: ParseFloat64
modules.header:
Reading a decimal float, and the failure every parser in this package reports.
`ParseError` lives here because this is where it was first needed, and it now serves every width: the integers,
the booleans, the characters and the wide floats all answer with it. Every case says where it was found, because
a reason on its own leaves a caller re-reading its own input to guess. "Invalid character" is a different report
from "invalid character at byte 7", and only the second lets anything underline what is wrong. The offsets are
into the text as given, so a parser embedded in a larger grammar adds the offset of the token it was handed and
the positions compose.
`OutOfMemory` is a correction rather than an addition. The wide float parser builds exact big integers to round
with, and every allocation those need used to be reported as `Overflow` — which told a caller their number was
too large when the machine had simply run out of room. The two want different responses from a caller, so they
are different cases.
The grammar this file accepts is `[+-]?(digits[.digits?]?|.digits)([eE][+-]?digits)?`, plus the two special
spellings `NaN` and `Inf` exactly as formatting writes them, so what one side prints the other reads.

modules.name: ParseInteger
modules.header:
Parsing an integer of any width, in any of the four bases.
One grammar serves every width: an optional sign, an optional base prefix — `0x`, `0o`, `0b`, exactly the
prefixes formatting writes under `#` — and digits of that base. The magnitude accumulates in `uint512`, the
widest integer there is, so one loop serves every width and overflow within the loop is impossible for any
narrower target; the width's own bound is checked once at the end, where the error can say which width refused.
The bound is one larger for a negative value, because the most negative value of every signed width has no
positive counterpart: `-128` fits an `int8` whose largest value is `127`.

modules.name: ParseValue
modules.header:
Parsing the two values whose text is a word or a character rather than digits.
A boolean is exactly `true` or `false` — not `True`, not `1`, not `yes`. Every widening of that set has to
choose which spellings count, and the choice differs by language and context; a caller wanting one applies it
before parsing, where the choice is visible.
A character is exactly one scalar value's encoding, whole: an empty string is not a character, and neither are
two of them.

modules.name: PrecisionDigits
modules.header:
Exactly the digits a precision asks for, rounded to nearest with ties to even.
The same exact ratio the shortest form is generated from, stopped on a digit count instead of on a distance to a
neighbour. That is Dragon4's fixed mode, and it matters that it is the same machinery: a fixed-precision
rendering produced by a different method could disagree with the shortest one about what the value is, and a
reader comparing `{}` against `{:.17}` would find two numbers.
It also matters that the digits come out of the ratio one at a time rather than out of `significand * 10^P`.
Ten to the eleven hundredth is 3,654 bits and would not fit the workspace at any precision worth supporting;
the remainder of a division never exceeds its divisor, so generating a thousand digits costs a thousand
iterations and no extra room at all. That is why the precision bound in Docs/NarrowFloat.md is a bound on the
output rather than on the arithmetic.
Rounding is where a fixed-precision renderer earns its keep. The tail past the last digit is still exactly held,
so "is it more than half" is a comparison rather than an estimate, and a tie is a tie rather than a value that
happened to land near one. Ties go to even, which is what reading the result back would do with it. A carry out
of the rounding can run the whole length of the digits — 9.99 at one decimal is 10.0, not 9.10 — so it is
propagated rather than applied to the last digit alone.

modules.name: Scientific
modules.header:
Scientific notation on request, and the two renderings a narrow float has that are not numbers.
`{:e}` and `{:E}` are the only styles a float understands. Each writes one digit before the point, the rest of
the digits after it, the mark, and the decimal exponent with its sign and at least two digits: `1.2345e+05`,
`2.5E-03`. That is the spelling `{}` already falls back to for a value too large or too small for fixed notation,
so a reader meets one scientific form whichever placeholder produced it. Without a precision the digits are the
shortest that read back as the same value, and a lone digit keeps a `.0` after it so the text still reads as a
float. With one, the precision counts the digits after the point, exactly, rounded to nearest with ties to even
by the same exact generator fixed precision uses; `.0` writes the single digit with no point.
A NaN or an infinity has no digits to place, so it renders as `NaN`, `Inf` or `-Inf` whatever the placeholder
asked for, and only the sign, width, fill and alignment of the specification apply to it.

modules.name: ShortestDigits
modules.header:
The shortest decimal that reads back as the same bits, found exactly.
This is the Steele and White method as Burger and Dybvig refined it, running on the fixed workspace next door.
Docs/NarrowFloat.md records why it and not one of the faster table-driven algorithms: those carry pre-computed
powers as data, and one of them carries a fallback path, and this package's rendering may neither allocate nor
have a path that behaves differently for inputs nobody tested.
The idea is one sentence. A binary float is not a decimal, so what a reader wants is not the value's exact
decimal expansion — 0.1 is really 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827, and printing that is true and useless —
but the shortest decimal that no other float is closer to. The value and the two gaps to its neighbours are held
as exact integer ratios, digits are generated one at a time, and generation stops the moment what has been
emitted is nearer to this value than to either neighbour. Nothing is approximated, so nothing has to be checked
afterwards.
The two asymmetries are where an implementation goes wrong, and both have cases in the test. A value at the
bottom of its binade is twice as far from its lower neighbour as from its upper one, because the exponent
changes underneath it, so the lower gap is half the width of the upper. And whether a decimal exactly on a gap
boundary is acceptable depends on whether the significand is even, because that is what round-to-nearest-even
would do with it when read back.

modules.name: Uint
modules.header: The decimal text of a `uint`.

modules.name: Uint16
modules.header: The decimal text of a `uint16`.

modules.name: Uint32
modules.header: The decimal text of a `uint32`.

modules.name: Uint64
modules.header: The decimal text of a `uint64`.

modules.name: Uint8
modules.header: The decimal text of a `uint8`.

modules.name: WideCharacterSlice
modules.header:
The UTF-16 and UTF-32 slices, transcoded on the way out.
A `char8[..]` renders by being copied: it is already the encoding the destination wants. Neither of these is, so
each needs a printer that decodes its units and writes UTF-8, and that is the whole reason they had none until
now. What the printer decides is what to do with the units that are not characters, and the answer is the one
every character width here already gives: `Display` replaces them with U+FFFD and `Debug` preserves them as
escapes carrying their own numbers.
The UTF-16 case is the one with structure. A scalar past U+FFFF is written as two units, a high half and a low
half, and only the pair means anything; a half on its own is not a character and never becomes one. So the
decoder reads a pair where there is one and reports a lone half where there is not, advancing a single unit
after it — which keeps a slice with one damaged unit in the middle of it readable on both sides of the damage.
Nothing here transcodes into a buffer first. A buffer would bound how long a slice may be, and a slice has no
bound, so the width a placeholder asks for is measured in one pass over the units and the padding is written
around the transcoding instead.

modules.name: WideDecimal
modules.header:
Decimal digits for a wide float, exactly.
The shortest rendering that reads back as the same value is found the way Steele and White, and then Burger and
Dybvig, described it: keep the exact value as a ratio of big integers, keep the exact distance to each
neighbouring float beside it, and generate digits until the digits so far sit closer to the value than to either
neighbour. Nothing is approximated, which is why it is correct at every width the same way, and why the numbers
involved are as large as the exponent makes them.
Fixed precision is the same machinery stopped at a chosen digit, with the remainder rounded to nearest and ties
to the even digit.
Both generators can fail two ways, and they say which. The allocator can refuse the working storage, which is
the machine rather than the value and may go differently on a second attempt; or the caller's digit buffer can
be too small for what the value needs, which will go the same way every time. Reporting both as one used to
tell a caller they were out of memory when their buffer was short — the same confusion the wide parser had
between an allocation failure and an overflow, and wrong for the same reason.

modules.name: WideFloat
modules.header:
The four wide IEEE formats, as values that carry their bits.
`float80`, `float128`, `float256` and `float512` are primitives with arithmetic of their own, but formatting needs
none of it. A float is an integer significand and a power of two, both of which sit in the bits as plain integer
fields, and turning them into decimal digits — or decimal digits back into them — is integer arithmetic all
the way down. So the values here are the bits, held in the integer width that fits, and every conversion below
reads and writes those fields directly.
A primitive crosses into one of these values through `FromValue` and back out through `Value`, which move the
bits and nothing else. The primitives get no `Display` of their own: the text allocates, and `FormatWith` on the
value is where a caller says from where.

modules.name: WideFloatParse
modules.header:
Reading decimal text into a wide float, exactly.
The grammar is the one `ParseFloat64` accepts, so what one width reads the others read. The conversion is not
the narrow one: every digit of the input is kept as an integer, the value is formed as a ratio of two integers
— the digits against a power of ten — and the quotient is taken to three bits past the precision with a
sticky bit for whatever remains. That is enough to round to nearest with ties to even without ever being wrong,
at any width, for any length of input.

modules.name: WideFloatText
modules.header:
Rendering a wide float the way `float64` renders, at any width.
The spelling is the narrow one exactly: `NaN`, `Inf`, a signed zero as `0.0`, fixed notation while the exponent
stays within what the digits can fill and scientific past it, and `{:.N}` as that many digits after the point.
A reader who knows what a `float64` looks like in text knows what these look like, which is the whole of the
design.
What differs is that the digits come from exact integer arithmetic rather than from a scaled double, so they
are the shortest that read back as the same bits at every width — and that the arithmetic needs an allocator,
because the numbers it works on are as large as the exponent makes them.

modules.name: WideFloatValue
modules.header:
The four wide widths as values: the bits, the questions a caller asks of them, and their text.
Each carries its bits in the narrowest integer that holds them, and answers `IsNan`, `IsInfinite`, `IsFinite`
and `IsNegative` from the fields directly. `FromValue` and `Value` move the bits to and from the primitive of
the same width through a raw pointer, the same boundary `BitsOfFloat64` crosses, since a cast would convert the
number rather than keep its representation.
None of them implements `Display` or `Debug`, and that absence is the design. Their text is found by exact
big-integer arithmetic that allocates — the narrow widths convert in a fixed workspace, but these are too wide
for one — and the protocols offer nowhere to pass an allocator. The four used to implement them anyway by
reaching for the system allocator, which put a hidden allocation behind an ordinary `{}` and gave a caller who
had chosen an allocator for everything else no way to make this follow. `FormatWith` takes one, and taking one
is the whole point: where a rendering allocates, the caller says from where.

modules.name: WideInt
modules.header:
The three integer widths past the machine word.
A `uint512` in decimal is one hundred fifty-five digits, and its digit loop is the same division loop every
narrower width uses — the arithmetic itself is the compiler's, which lowers wide division natively. What differs
per width is only the type the loop runs in, so each width carries its loop and everything after the digits is
shared with the narrow widths through `WriteIntegerDigits`.
The magnitude of a negative value is taken in the unsigned counterpart, for the reason the narrow widths do it:
the most negative value of any signed width has no positive counterpart to negate into, and two's complement in
the unsigned type is right for it and for every other value.

Writes `format` into `writer`, with each `{}` replaced by the next argument.
A placeholder is `{}`, or `{:spec}` carrying fill, alignment, sign, width, precision and style — see
`ParseFormatSpec` for the grammar. `{{` and `}}` stand for a literal brace, and are the only way to write one.
The pattern is checked before any of it is written, so a pattern that is wrong produces no output rather than a
prefix of one. What is checked is the pattern and the argument count, both of which are known at the call site;
a value's own rendering can still fail partway, and what it managed to write stays written. `format` is marked
`#Format()`, so when it is a string literal the compiler counts its placeholders against the arguments and a
mismatch is reported while compiling rather than as `ArgumentCountMismatch`.
Reports `InvalidSpecification` with the byte offset into `format` for a specification that does not parse, a
brace the grammar does not allow, or a placeholder with no closing brace; `ArgumentCountMismatch` with the
placeholders counted and the arguments supplied when the two differ; and otherwise whatever the destination or
a value's own renderer reported, stopping at the first refusal. The first two are found before anything is
written.
doc.returns: success when the whole pattern and every argument were accepted

items.name: Render
items.signature: pub func Render(allocator: Allocator, #Format() format: char8[..], ...) -> String ! FormatError

doc.summary: The text `format` becomes with its placeholders filled, as a string of its own.
doc.markdown:
The text `format` becomes with its placeholders filled, as a string of its own.
This is the allocating entry point, and the only one: every other way of rendering writes into a destination the
caller already has. Reserving up front is a guess at the result's size — the literal text plus a little for each
argument — so a short call fills in without a reallocation and a long one grows through the builder as usual.
It is named for what it does rather than for the package, because `Format(allocator, ...)` read as a noun and a
namespace at once and said nothing about producing a value.
Reports `TextFailure(OutOfMemory)` when the initial reservation fails, and otherwise whatever `WriteFormat`
reported. On failure the partially built string is released rather than returned, so a caller never receives
half a rendering that looks whole and the allocator gets its block back either way.

doc.summary: Why text could not be read as a value.
doc.markdown:
Why text could not be read as a value.
Failure-only: every case is a failure, and each says where in the text it was found. Success is the other channel
of the `T ! ParseError` a parser returns rather than a case here.
Copy, carrying one offset.

cases.name: Empty
cases.doc: There were no bytes to read. The offset is zero, which is both the start of the text and its length.

cases.name: InvalidCharacter
cases.doc:
A byte that is not part of the grammar, or a well-formed value with something after it. The offset is that
byte, which is the text's length when the value stopped short.

cases.name: Overflow
cases.doc:
The value is well formed and does not fit the width asked for. The offset is the digit that passed the
widest representable magnitude, or the end of the number when the number itself is what does not fit.

cases.name: OutOfMemory
cases.doc:
The exact arithmetic a wide float needs could not get the storage for it. This is the machine rather than
the text: the same input on a less busy machine reads fine, which is what tells it apart from `Overflow`.
The offset is where the parser had reached, which is the end of the number.

doc.summary: Reads the decimal grammar out of `str`, without deciding what float it names.
doc.markdown:
Reads the decimal grammar out of `str`, without deciding what float it names.
One scanner for both narrow widths, so what one reads the other reads: the grammar is
`[+-]?(digits[.digits?]?|.digits)([eE][+-]?digits)?`, plus the two special spellings `NaN` and `Inf` exactly as
formatting writes them. The digits are kept exactly up to `RetainedDecimalDigits`, past which a nonzero one
sets `truncated` and moves the exponent instead.

`OutOfMemory` where the retained digits would not fit the workspace.

length for a value past the largest finite `float64` — refused rather than rounded to an infinity, since that
would turn a number the caller wrote into one they did not. A value below the smallest subnormal is the signed
zero it rounds to.

items.name: PrecisionDigits
items.signature: pub func PrecisionDigits(significand: uint64, exponent: int, precision: uint, into: var char8[..], count: *var uint, power: *var int) -> bool

doc.summary:
Writes the digits of `significand * 2^exponent` down to the place `precision` names, rounded to nearest with
ties to even.
doc.markdown:
Writes the digits of `significand * 2^exponent` down to the place `precision` names, rounded to nearest with
ties to even.
The digits are the significant ones with no point and no sign, and `power` receives the exponent that places
them: the value is `0.d1d2...dn * 10^power`, so the last digit written stands for `10^-precision`. A value
small enough that nothing reaches that place produces no digits and a power of zero, which the caller writes
as a zero and a tail of zeros.
Answers false when `precision` is past `MaximumPrecision`, when `into` is too short for the digits the value
needs, or when the exact arithmetic could not run in the fixed workspace — which Docs/NarrowFloat.md proves the
narrow widths do not reach.

doc.summary: Writes a finite float in fixed notation with exactly `precision` digits after the decimal point.
doc.markdown:
Writes a finite float in fixed notation with exactly `precision` digits after the decimal point.
Always fixed notation, because that is the only notation in which "digits after the decimal point" has one
meaning. A large value therefore renders with every integer digit it has and then the fraction — which is what
was asked for, and why the precision is bounded rather than the output.
Answers false when the precision is past `MaximumPrecision`, or when the exact arithmetic could not run in the
fixed workspace. There is no fallback to another rendering: a refused request is refused.

items.name: WriteScientificNotation
items.signature: pub func WriteScientificNotation(writer: &var TextWriter, spec: FormatSpec, parts: FloatParts, mark: char8) -> ! FormatError

doc.summary:
Renders a finite float in scientific notation under `spec`, and applies the specification's sign, width, fill and
alignment to the result.
doc.markdown:
Renders a finite float in scientific notation under `spec`, and applies the specification's sign, width, fill and
alignment to the result.
One digit comes before the point and the rest after it, then `mark` and the decimal exponent with its sign and at
least two digits: `1.2345e+05`. Without a precision the digits are the shortest that read back as the same
value, with `.0` after a lone digit; with one, the precision counts the digits after the point, rounded to
nearest with ties to even, and `.0` writes no point at all. A zero is `0.0e+00`, keeping the sign of a negative
zero.
Reports `UnsupportedRequest` for a precision past `MaximumPrecision`, and whatever the writer reported otherwise.
There is no fallback: a refused precision produces no output.
doc.returns: success when the whole rendering was accepted

items.name: MaximumShortestDigits
items.signature: pub const MaximumShortestDigits: uint

doc.summary: The most digits a shortest rendering can need.
doc.markdown:
The most digits a shortest rendering can need.
Seventeen for a `float64` and nine for a `float32`: those are the counts at which every value of the width is
distinguishable from every other, which is the theoretical bound on how long a shortest form can be. The buffer
a caller supplies is checked against this rather than against a guess.

items.name: ShortestDigits
items.signature: pub func ShortestDigits(significand: uint64, exponent: int, atBinadeBottom: bool, into: var char8[..], count: *var uint, exponent10: *var int) -> bool

doc.summary: Writes the shortest decimal digits of `significand * 2^exponent` that read back to exactly that value.
doc.markdown:
Writes the shortest decimal digits of `significand * 2^exponent` that read back to exactly that value.
The digits are the significant ones with no point and no sign: `into` receives them most significant first,
`count` how many there are, and `exponent10` the power of ten the first of them stands for, so the value is
`0.d1d2...dn * 10^(exponent10 + 1)` and the caller places the point.
`atBinadeBottom` says the value is the smallest significand of its exponent, whose lower neighbour is half as
far away as its upper one. A caller reading a `float64` passes true when the stored mantissa is zero and the
biased exponent is above one.
Answers false when `into` is shorter than `MaximumShortestDigits`, or when the workspace could not hold the
arithmetic — which Docs/NarrowFloat.md proves the narrow widths do not reach, so a false from that cause is a
defect in the bound rather than an input to handle. Nothing partial is reported: `count` is zero on failure.
